Where it began

Robin Arnold Smith was born in Durban on 13 September 1963 and went to Northwood School, which later named its first-team cricket ground after him. Like his older brother Chris, he could not play for the land of his birth, because South Africa was shut out of international cricket at the time. His parents were British, though, and that opened the door to England.

He made his home at Hampshire, winning three one-day trophies with them: the Benson and Hedges Cup (1988 and again 1992) and the NatWest Trophy (1991).

The player

Smith's first Test came at Headingley in 1988, against a fearsome West Indies attack, and he marked it with a century stand alongside Allan Lamb, a fellow South African-born batter. A year later he was the one England batter to prosper in the 1989 Ashes, making two hundreds. At Trent Bridge he walked out with England three down and 600 behind, and went on the attack.

His best Test score, 175 against West Indies in Antigua, came in reply to Brian Lara's record 375. Across 62 Tests from 1988 to 1996 he scored 4,236 runs at 43.67, with nine hundreds and 28 fifties. He was also in the England side that reached the final of the 1992 World Cup, and his unbeaten 167 against Australia at Edgbaston in 1993 stood as England's best one-day innings until 2016.

What made him special

Fast bowling brought out the best in him. He was famous for standing up to the quickest bowlers in the world, and for a square cut he hit with real ferocity. He was counted among England's bravest players, and the West Indies quicks found out how hard he was to shift.

Slow bowling was a different conversation. Spinners, Shane Warne among them, gave him more to think about, which only goes to show that even the bravest batter has a ball he would rather not face.

Away from the middle

When he grew his hair long, people thought he looked like a judge, and the nickname Judge, or Judgie, stuck. He captained Hampshire from 1998 to 2002 and won the man of the match award in two of their one-day finals. He was a Wisden Cricketer of the Year. After his playing days he moved to Australia, helped run the helmet makers Masuri, worked for his brother's clothing company, ran a cricket academy of his own and studied psychological science at Swinburne University in Melbourne. He died on 1 December 2025, aged 62.

And finally

He bowled in Tests without ever taking a wicket. Given the way he treated other people's bowling, perhaps that was only fair.
